en: The Great Exposition (Mahāniddesa),
Chapter on the Eights (Aṭṭhakavagga), 9.
The Exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta (Māgaṇḍiyasuttaniddesa)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta:
"Having seen craving, aversion, and lust,
there was no desire even for sexual intercourse."
"What is this thing filled with urine and excrement,
that one would not even wish to touch it with the feet?
Having seen through craving, aversion, and lust, there was no longer any desire even for sexual union."
Having seen and beheld Taṇhā, Aratī, and Rāgā—the daughters of Māra—there was no desire, no lust, nor any affection for sexual intercourse.
Having seen them, there was no desire even for sexual union.
"What is this, filled with urine and excrement? One would not wish even to touch it with one's feet."
Why indeed would one not wish to tread with the foot upon this body, which is full of urine, full of excrement, full of phlegm, full of blood;
a collection of bones bound together by sinews, smeared with blood and flesh, wrapped in skin, covered by the outer hide,
riddled with holes, oozing and trickling, infested by swarms of worms, and filled with various kinds of filth?
"But how could there be cohabitation or meeting?"—thinking, "What is this?
It is filled with urine and excrement; one would not even wish to touch it with one's feet.
And it is no wonder that a human being, longing for divine pleasures, would not desire human pleasures, or one longing for human pleasures would not desire divine pleasures.
"What is your view when you neither desire, nor accept, nor long for, nor yearn for, nor crave both of these? With what kind of view are you endowed?
Thus the Blessed One asked, and said:
"Having seen craving, aversion, and lust..."
"I had no desire even for sexual intercourse;
why indeed would I wish to touch with my feet this thing filled with urine and excrement?"
If you do not desire such a jewel as this—
a woman sought after by many lords of men—
then what is the point of this life lived in mere views or in the observance of mere rules?
"And you speak of the kind of rebirth one undergoes. 'I say this'—
such a thought does not occur to him," [said the Blessed One, "O Māgaṇḍiya"].
Having discerned among phenomena what was firmly grasped,
and seeing through views without clinging,
I beheld the inner peace that I had cultivated.
‘I say this’ does not occur to him.
‘I say this’: “I say this,” “I say that,” “I say so much,” “I say to this extent,” “I say this speculative view:
‘The world is eternal,’” or... [and so on].
“Or: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
“It does not belong to him” means: “It does not belong to me”; “It does not belong to him” means: “I do not say, ‘To this extent I speak’”—it does not belong to him.
"Māgaṇḍiya," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for reverence... [as before] ...it is a realization-based description, namely, "the Blessed One"—thus, "Māgaṇḍiya, the Blessed One."
"Having thoroughly determined among the phenomena":
"among the phenomena" means among the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"Having thoroughly determined" means having determined, having analyzed, having investigated, having scrutinized, having weighed, having judged, having clarified, and having made manifest.

"Grasped at" means: grasped by way of a downward sweep, grasped by way of a cavity, grasped by way of a choice, grasped by way of parts, grasped by way of accumulation, grasped by way of total accumulation;
that which is taken up, adhered to, settled upon, clung to, and intent upon [with the thought], "This is true, this is real, this is such, this is become, this is as it is, this is non-perverted."

"It does not exist, it is not present, it is not found, it is not obtained; it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge"—thus one should discern what has been grasped among phenomena.
And seeing thus, one should not cling to views.
Seeing the danger in views, I do not grasp at views, I do not misapprehend them, and I do not adhere to them.
Or rather: they are not to be grasped, not to be misapprehended, and not to be adhered to. Seeing thus, one does not take up views.
Or else, the view that "the world is eternal;

this alone is true, all else is false" is a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a snare of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views—accompanied by suffering, vexation, despair, and feverish distress;
it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment.
"It does not lead to full awakening, nor does it lead to Nibbāna.
Seeing the danger in views, I do not grasp at views, I do not misapprehend them, and I do not adhere to them.
Or rather, [I see that] they should not be grasped, they should not be misapprehended, and they should not be adhered to.
Thus one should see, without adhering to views. Or alternatively: "The world is eternal;
the world is finite; the world is infinite; the soul and the body are identical; the soul is one thing and the body another;
a Tathāgata exists after death; a Tathāgata does not exist after death; [a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death]."
“The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—this alone is the truth, all else is vain.
This is a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views;
it is accompanied by suffering, distress, despair, and fever.
"It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
Seeing the danger in views, I do not grasp at them, I do not cling to them, and I do not adhere to them.
Or alternatively: "They are not to be grasped, not to be misapprehended, and not to be adhered to"—thus one views them without favoring views.
Or alternatively: "These views, when thus grasped and thus misapprehended, will lead to such a destination and such a future state."
Seeing the danger in views, I do not grasp at views, I do not misapprehend them, and I do not adhere to them.
Or rather: they are not to be grasped, not to be misapprehended, and not to be adhered to.
Thus, while seeing in this way, one does not hold to views.
Alternatively, these views lead to hell, lead to the animal realm, and lead to the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Seeing the danger in views, I do not take them up, I do not misapprehend them, and I do not adhere to them.
Or rather, they are not to be taken up, not to be misapprehended, and not to be adhered to.
Thus he sees, without being supported by views.
Or else, he sees: "These views are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Seeing the danger in views, he does not grasp at views, does not misapprehend them, and does not adhere to them.
Or alternatively: "They should not be grasped, they should not be clung to, they should not be adhered to.
Thus, by seeing in this way and by not favoring views, one cultivates internal peace and does not look outward.
Internal peace: internal peace from lust, peace from hatred, peace from delusion, peace from anger,
resentment, contempt, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, hostility, conceit,
arrogance, vanity, negligence, and from all defilements.

...the peace, the subsiding, the allaying, the extinction, the tranquilization of all misconduct ... of all distresses ... of all fevers ... of all torments ... of all unwholesome volitional formations. While heaping them up, heaping them up;
sorting them out, sorting them out; discriminating, discriminating; weighing, weighing; scrutinizing, scrutinizing; making them manifest, making them manifest, [he sees] their peace.
“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’— while collecting, sorting, discerning, weighing, determining, and fully clarifying this, making it manifest;
‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘all phenomena are non-self’— while collecting, sorting, discerning …”
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”— thus reflecting, discerning, thoroughly discerning, weighing, scrutinizing,
clarifying, and making manifest. “I saw, I beheld, I looked upon, I perceived, I penetrated”—
reflecting on internal peace, I beheld it.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“‘I say this’ does not occur to him,” (O Māgaṇḍiya,
said the Blessed One).
Having discerned what is grasped among phenomena,
and seeing while not clinging to views,
one cultivates internal peace through non-seeing.
"Those various legal judgments that have been formulated," said Māgaṇḍiya, "those you,
O Sage, call 'without grasping'."
"How is it that this matter called 'inner peace' has been proclaimed by the wise?
What are those determinations that have been formulated?"
"Decisions" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views; they are called "decisions of views.
"Formulated" means fashioned, well-fashioned, constructed, and established—thus they are "formulated.

Alternatively, they are "formulated" in the sense that they are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to transformation.
"Those decisions which have been formulated.
Thus, "Māgaṇḍiya. "Thus" (iti) refers to this:
the connection of words, the conjunction of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words.
"Thus": *Māgaṇḍiya* is the name, designation, appellation, and conventional term for that brahmin—
thus, "Māgaṇḍiya."
"Those indeed, O Sage, you speak of without grasping, as 'inner peace'—this is the meaning. Regarding "those":
it refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views. "Muni" (the Sage) refers to the Buddha.
"Mona" is said to be knowledge... [as before] ... "having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage.
"Without grasping": you say, "seeing the danger in views, I do not grasp at views, I do not misapprehend them, I do not adhere to them," and you also say, "I am inwardly peaceful.
"This which is the meaning": that which is the ultimate meaning.
"Those indeed you call 'sages' out of favor, regarding this matter as 'inner peace.
How, indeed, has that teaching been proclaimed by the wise?

The phrase 'how, indeed' (*kathaṃ nu*) is a question of doubt, a question of perplexity, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision; it is: 'Is it thus?', 'Is it not thus?', 'What then?', 'How then?'"
"How indeed? means:
"by the wise" means by those who are steadfast, learned, possessed of wisdom, endowed with intelligence, knowledgeable, discerning, sagacious, and insightful.
"Proclaimed" means known; it is proclaimed, announced, taught, made known, established, disclosed, analyzed, clarified, and revealed.
How indeed was that proclaimed by the wise?
Therefore, that brahmin said:
"Those determinations which have been fashioned..."
(Thus said Māgaṇḍiya:
"Those indeed you call sages out of favor;
this matter that you state as 'inner peace'—"
“How, then, has it been proclaimed by the wise?
“Not through view, not through hearsay, nor through knowledge,” said the Blessed One, “Māgaṇḍiya.”
He did not say that purity comes through rules and observances;
nor does it come through lack of wrong views, lack of learning,
lack of knowledge, lack of virtue, or lack of observances.
Having relinquished these and not grasping at them,
the peaceful one, being independent,
should not yearn for existence. Not through view, nor through hearsay, nor through knowledge.
You do not say, speak, declare, illuminate, or express purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation through what is seen;
nor do you say, speak, declare, illuminate, or express purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation through what is heard;
nor do you say, speak, declare, illuminate, or express purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation through what is both seen and heard.

“By knowledge as well, you do not declare, nor speak of, nor state, nor illuminate, nor express purification, complete purification, utter purification, liberation, complete liberation, or total liberation”—
that is, neither by view, nor by hearsay, nor by knowledge.
“Māgaṇḍiya,” the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-designation, namely "Bhagavā"—
thus he said, "Māgaṇḍiya, one does not attain purity even through rules and observances."

"I do not say, nor do I speak, nor do I declare, nor do I illuminate, nor do I express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation comes through moral discipline (*sīla*);

nor do I say, nor do I speak, nor do I declare, nor do I illuminate, nor do I express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation comes through virtuous conduct (*vata*);

nor do I say, nor do I speak, nor do I declare, nor do I illuminate, nor do I express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation comes through both moral discipline and virtuous conduct (*sīlabbata*)."
He does not say that purity comes through rules and observances either:
"Neither by wrong view, nor by lack of learning, nor by ignorance, nor by lack of virtue, nor by lack of observance is there purity.
Thus, right view must also be sought.
Right view with ten bases:
there is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of wholesome and unwholesome deeds;
there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings of spontaneous birth.
"There are in the world recluses and brahmins who have gone rightly and practiced rightly, who,
having personally realized this world and the other world through direct knowledge, make them known";
even the hearing of such a report is to be desired.

The voice of another, discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" sayings, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and questions-and-answers;
and knowledge is also to be sought— namely, the knowledge of action as one's own property, the knowledge in conformity with the truths, direct knowledge, and the knowledge of meditative attainments.
Virtue is also to be desired—
the restraint of the Pātimokkha;
conduct is also to be desired.
The eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are:

the practice of dwelling in the forest, the practice of eating only almsfood, the practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of possessing only three robes, the practice of walking for alms in regular order, the practice of refusing food offered after the proper time, the practice of remaining in the sitting posture, and the practice of accepting whatever seat is assigned.
It is not by lack of right view, lack of learning, or lack of knowledge, nor by lack of virtue or lack of conduct, that one is [defiled] thereby.

One does not attain inner peace through right view alone, nor through mere hearing, nor through mere knowledge, nor through mere virtue, nor through mere observance of vows; yet one does not reach inner peace without these qualities.

Nevertheless, these qualities are the requisites for attaining, achieving, touching, and realizing inner peace—not by means of no view, no hearing, no knowledge, no virtue, and no vows, nor even by that [absence] alone.
"And having relinquished these, one should not grasp them.
Here, "these" refers to the states belonging to the dark side, the relinquishing of which through their eradication is to be desired;
and non-identification with the wholesome states pertaining to the three realms is to be desired, whereby the states belonging to the dark side are abandoned by means of that eradication-abandonment.
They have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Regarding wholesome states belonging to the three elements, there is a lack of identification; to this extent, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere.
Or rather, [one understands]: "These are not to be grasped, not to be misapprehended, and not to be adhered to."
Thus, having relinquished these and not grasping them—

since craving, views, and conceit have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future— one does not grasp, does not misapprehend,
and does not adhere even to this extent. Thus, having relinquished these and not grasping them.
When the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future— then even to that extent one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere. Thus,
having relinquished these and not grasping them...
The peaceful one, not relying on existence, does not yearn for it.
"Peaceful" means he is peaceful because of the subsiding of lust, peaceful because of the subsiding of hatred, peaceful because of the subsiding of delusion;
[he is peaceful] because of the subsiding of anger … resentment … contempt … insolence … envy … avarice … deceit … [and so forth].

Because of the subsiding, the calming, the pacifying, the extinguishing, and the quenching of deceitfulness... of stubbornness... of aggression... of conceit... of arrogance... of intoxication... of negligence... of all defilements...
of all misconduct... of all distresses... of all fevers... of all torments... and of all unwholesome volitional formations.
Because he is free from [defilements], because he is calmed, stilled, tranquil, extinguished, and pacified, he is "peaceful" (*santo*).
"Without dependence" (*anissāya*): there are two kinds of dependence.
The dependence on craving and the dependence on views... [as before] ...this is the dependence on craving...
[as before] ...this is the dependence on views.
Having abandoned reliance on craving and relinquished reliance on views, he does not rely on the eye, does not rely on the ear, does not rely on the nose,
does not rely on the tongue, does not rely on the body, and does not rely on the mind; nor does he rely on forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clans, assemblies, dwellings, gains, fame, or praise.

pleasure … robes … almsfood … lodgings … medicinal requisites for the sick … the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm … the immaterial realm … existence in the sense sphere … existence in the fine-material sphere … existence in the immaterial sphere … existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence.
… not relying on, not grasping, not adhering to, and not becoming obsessed with past phenomena, future phenomena, present phenomena,
or phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—
this is called "peaceful, not relying."

One does not yearn for existence; one should not yearn for sense-sphere existence, one should not yearn for fine-material existence, one should not yearn for immaterial existence—one should not long for it, should not crave for it, should not obsess over it.
Thus, being peaceful and independent, one does not yearn for existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Neither by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge, (Māgaṇḍiya,
said the Blessed One),
nor even by rules and observances, does one speak of purity;”
Through wrong view, lack of learning, ignorance, lack of virtue,
and lack of restraint— one does not [attain the goal] by those means;
having relinquished these and being without grasping, [one attains it].
“The noble one, not being dependent, does not yearn for existence.
“If it is not by means of view, nor by means of hearsay, nor by means of knowledge,” said Māgandiya.
He did not say that purity comes through rules and observances;
nor does it come through lack of wrong views, lack of learning,
lack of knowledge, lack of virtue, or lack of observances.
"I think that the Dhamma is indeed bewildering;
some declare purification through views,
yet it is not indeed by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge."

You do not claim, nor do you state, nor do you speak of, nor do you illuminate, nor do you express, purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation through view;
nor [do you so claim] through hearing... nor [do you so claim] through what is seen and heard... purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation.

"By knowledge as well, you do not declare, nor do you speak of, nor do you state, nor do you illuminate, nor do you express purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, complete liberation, or total liberation"—if indeed it is not by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge.
Thus, "Māgaṇḍiya," [the word] *iti* is a grammatical connection... [and so on].
"Māgaṇḍiya" is the name of that brahmin...
thus he is called Māgaṇḍiya.
"One does not attain purity even through rules and observances."

"I do not say, nor do I speak, nor do I declare, nor do I illuminate, nor do I express that purity, purification, and complete purification through virtue (*sīla*); ... nor purity, purification, and complete purification through conduct (*vata*); ... nor purity, purification, and complete purification through both virtue and conduct; nor liberation, emancipation, and total release."
He does not say that purity comes through rules and observances either: "Neither by wrong view, nor by lack of learning, nor by ignorance, nor by lack of virtue, nor by lack of observances.
You say that right view is desirable; you say that hearing is desirable; you say that knowledge is desirable. Thus, you cannot categorically affirm it, nor can you categorically reject it.
“Because of not seeing, not hearing, not knowing, because of lack of virtue, and lack of conduct—it is not by that [means].
I consider this to be merely a state of delusion (*momuha-dhamma*).

‘This is your state of delusion, your state of folly, your state of confusion, your state of ignorance, your state of eternal wrangling (*amarāvikkhepa*)’—thus I conceive, thus I know, thus I understand, thus I discern, thus I penetrate, thus I pierce through.”
I consider this teaching to be utterly bewildering.
Some declare purity through a particular view.
On account of their view of purity, some ascetics and brahmins declare that there is purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.

“‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—by means of such a view, some recluses and brahmins claim purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.

‘The world is not eternal … [and so on] … after death a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is true, all else is false’—by means of such a view, some recluses and brahmins claim purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.”
Some declare purification through views.
Therefore that brahmin said:
"If indeed it is not by view, nor by learning, nor by knowledge..."
(Thus said Māgaṇḍiya:
He did not say that purity comes even through rules and observances;
nor [does it come] from lack of wrong view, lack of learning, or lack of knowledge.
“Neither by lack of virtue nor by non-observance of vows do they attain purity;
I consider that to be merely a deluded teaching,
for some declare purification through mere views.”
"O Māgaṇḍiya," said the Blessed One, "by questioning while relying on views,
you have fallen into confusion regarding those things that have been grasped."
And herein you did not perceive even the slightest perception;
therefore, out of sheer delusion, you maintain your view while being questioned. Thus it was said.
The brahmin Māgaṇḍiya asks about views based on views; he asks about attachments based on attachments; he asks about fetters based on fetters; he asks about impediments based on impediments.
“Inquiring again and again” means he inquires repeatedly—thus, “inquiring again and again based on views.”
“Māgaṇḍiya,” said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
“Blessed One” (bhagavā) is a designation for veneration... [as before] ...it is a realization-based designation, namely, “Blessed One”—thus, “Māgaṇḍiya,” said the Blessed One.
"You have fallen into delusion regarding what you have grasped.
That view which was taken up by you—clung to, adhered to, settled upon, and intent upon—it is by that very view that you are bewildered, utterly bewildered, completely bewildered;
you have come to delusion, come to utter delusion, come to total delusion."
"You have plunged into darkness"—
you have fallen into delusion regarding what you have grasped;
for from this, you do not perceive even the slightest sign.

Whether from this internal state, or from the path, or from the teaching of the Dhamma, he does not obtain the perception of what is appropriate, the perception of what has been attained, the perception of characteristics, the perception of causes, or the perception of the proper occasion; how then could there be knowledge?
Thus, he did not perceive even the slightest perception from this.

Or alternatively, he does not obtain even the mere arising of a perception or the mere act of perceiving that which is impermanent or conforms to the perception of impermanence, that which is suffering or conforms to the perception of suffering, or that which is non-self or conforms to the perception of non-self; how then could there be knowledge?
"Even thus, you did not perceive even the slightest perception from this [state].
Therefore, you have been burnt by delusion.
"Therefore" means: for that reason, on that account, by that cause, by that condition, by that source—that is, due to the nature of delusion, due to the nature of folly.
Because you perceive, see, will see, look at, contemplate, and examine from a state of delusion,
from a state of ignorance, and from a state of endless equivocation—
therefore, you perceive from a state of confusion.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“While questioning me while relying on views,
(‘Māgaṇḍiya,’ said the Blessed One),”
"You have fallen into confusion regarding what was grasped;
you did not perceive even the slightest sign from this [reality].
Therefore, you have caused me to be bewildered."
Only one who considers himself superior or inferior would dispute with such a person;
but one who is unshakable regarding these three states—
"Equal, he thinks himself superior;
equal, or even inferior—whosoever conceives thus, he would dispute with him.
Whosoever conceives, "I am equal," or "I am superior," or "I am inferior," he [disputes] by means of that conceit.
On account of that view or with that person, one might engage in quarreling, brawling, contention, dispute, or strife, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya. What do you know about this?"
“You do not understand the Dhamma and Vinaya; you have practiced wrongly, whereas I have practiced rightly. What is consistent for me is inconsistent for you.
You spoke last what should have been spoken first, and you spoke first what should have been spoken last.
Your established position has been overturned; your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to save your argument, or disentangle yourself if you can.”
He who conceives himself as equal, superior, or inferior would dispute with that [other].
But for one who is unshakable regarding these three modes, the thought "I am equal" or "I am superior" does not occur.
For him by whom these three modes have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising by the fire of knowledge—
Burnt away, he does not waver or tremble in the three modes; for that person who does not waver, there is no thought:
"I am equal," or "I am superior," or "I am inferior.
For him, it does not exist.
Unshaken in the three modes, he is neither "equal" nor "superior"— such [distinctions] do not exist for him.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whether equal, superior, or inferior,
he who conceives such thoughts would dispute with him;
but one who is unshakable regarding these three conditions— ”
"Only the distinguished one has it"—
what could that brahmin say regarding truth,
or with whom could he dispute about falsehood?
In whom there is neither the even nor the uneven,
with whom could he engage in debate?
What could that brahmin say regarding "truth"?
"A Brahmin" is one who has banished seven qualities, and is thus a Brahmin... [as it is said] "...unattached, such a one is called a Brahmā.

"What would that Brahmin say?"—what would the Brahmin say, what would he speak, what would he declare, what would he illuminate, what would he assert, namely: "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false"?

“The world is eternal”… “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”—what would that brahmin say, what would he speak, what would he declare, what would he illuminate, what would he assert?
That brahmin would say: “This is true.”

"Or how could he dispute, saying 'It is false for you, it is true for me'? By what conceit, by what view, or with what person would one engage in quarreling, brawling, contention, dispute, or strife, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... [and so forth]..."
"Or if you are able, explain it away"—
with such words as "it is false," with what could he dispute?
For in that [state] there is neither the even nor the uneven.
In whichever person—an Arahant whose taints are exhausted—there is no conceit of "I am equal," no conceit of "I am superior," and no self-depreciation of "I am inferior";
which do not exist, are not found, and are not perceived;
which have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; which are incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge—this is [the case].
"In whom there is neither evenness nor unevenness—
who would he engage in dispute?
With what conceit, with what view, or with what person would he engage in dispute, be capable of dispute, or create a quarrel, a contention, a conflict, a strife, or a tumult?"
“If you do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline...
[as before] ...or unravel it if you are able”—
with whom would he engage in debate?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"What could that brahmin say regarding 'truth,' or with whom could he dispute regarding 'falsehood'?"
In whom there is neither evenness nor unevenness—
who would engage in dispute with him?
Having abandoned his dwelling, he wanders without a home.
The sage who forms no intimacies in the village,
being free from sensual desires and seeking nothing for himself—
how could he engage in dispute with people?
Then the householder Hāliddakāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the householder Hāliddakāni said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
“Bhante Kaccāna, this was said by the Blessed One in the *Aṭṭhakavagga*, in the *Māgaṇḍiya-pañha*:”
Having abandoned home, wandering without a fixed abode,
the sage forms no intimacies in the village;
empty of sensual desires, he looks forward to nothing.
“How should one not engage in dispute with people?
“Venerable Kaccāna, how should the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One be understood in detail?
“Householder, the form-element is the abode of consciousness; and consciousness, being bound by craving for the form-element, is said to be a wanderer in its abode.”
The element of feeling, householder...
the element of perception, householder...

the element of volitional formations, householder, is the abode of consciousness; and because consciousness is bound by craving for the element of volitional formations, it is said that consciousness "wanders about in its abode."
In this way, householder, one is a wanderer in a dwelling.
And how, householder, is one a non-wanderer in a dwelling?
Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever clinging and grasping of the mind there is toward the realm of form, householder—
Those underlying tendencies toward dogmatic adherence and insistence have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future;
therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be one who does not dwell in a home.
In the case of the element of feeling, householder...
in the case of the element of perception, householder...
in the case of the element of volitional formations, householder...
Householder, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, clinging, grasping, mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendencies there are regarding the consciousness element—
all these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called one who dwells without a home.
In this way, householder, one is a dweller without a home.
And how, householder, is one a dweller with a home?
Householder, one who wanders among dwellings, being bound by the outward diffusion toward the signs of forms, is called a "wanderer among dwellings.
[The same applies to] the sign of sounds...
the sign of odors... [and so forth].

Householder, one who wanders through the attachment and bondage of spreading out from the dwelling in the signs of taste, the signs of tangibles, and the signs of mental phenomena, is called "one who wanders in a dwelling."
In this way, householder, one wanders with a home.
And how, householder, does one wander without a home?

For the Tathāgata, householder, the wandering and bondage within the home of the sign of form have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called one who wanders without a home.
[The same applies to] the sign of sound … the sign of fragrance … [the sign of taste … the sign of touch … the sign of mental phenomena].

Householder, the Tathāgata has abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to future non-arising, the attachment and bondage of wandering in the dwellings of the signs of tastes, the signs of tangibles, and the signs of mental phenomena.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called one who wanders without a home.
In this way, householder, one wanders without a home.
And how, householder, does one become intimate with the village?

"Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu dwells in close association with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows; he is happy when they are happy and sorrowful when they are sorrowful, and he exerts himself personally whenever duties or tasks arise for them.
It is in this way, householder, that one becomes intimate with the village.
And how, householder, does one not become intimate with the village?"
"Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu dwells unassociated with householders; he does not share their joys, nor their sorrows;
he is not happy when they are happy, nor distressed when they are distressed; and when there are duties or tasks that have arisen, he does not personally involve himself in them.
It is in this way, householder, that one is not born of intimacy in the village."
And how, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures?

Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he is not devoid of desire, not devoid of affection, not devoid of thirst, not devoid of fever, and not devoid of craving for them.
It is in this way, householder, that one is empty of sensual pleasures.
And how, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures?
Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu is free from passion for sensual pleasures; he is devoid of desire, devoid of affection, devoid of thirst, devoid of fever, and devoid of craving.
It is in this way, householder, that one is empty of sensual pleasures.
And how, householder, is one forward-looking?
Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu thinks thus:
"May I be of such a form in the future," and so forth.
‘May I have such feeling… may I have such perception… may I have such volitional formations…’
‘May I have such consciousness in the future’—
in this way, householder, one has expectations.
And how, householder, does one have no expectations?
"Here, householder, it does not occur to a certain bhikkhu:
‘May I be of such a form in the future,’ nor:
‘May I be of such a feeling…'"
‘May I have such perception in the future… may I have such volitional formations in the future… may I have such consciousness in the future.’…
In this way, householder, one is not forward.
And how, householder, does one engage in dispute with people?
Here, householder, a certain person engages in such talk as this: [he says]...
‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline.
How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. My [practice] is consistent; yours is inconsistent.
What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. You have overstepped [the bounds].’
"You have been turned upside down; your position has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to rescue your argument, or disentangle yourself if you can!
In this way, householder, one is a maker of strife with people.
And how, householder, is one not a maker of strife with people?
In this case, householder, a certain person does not engage in such speech as:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline... [etc.
...or unravel it if you are able.”
"In this way, householder, one does not engage in quarreling with people.
Thus, householder, as for that which was said by the Blessed One in the *Māgaṇḍiya-pañha* of the *Aṭṭhaka-vagga*:
'Having abandoned the home, wandering without a fixed abode...'"
“The sage who makes no intimacies in the village,
devoid of sensual desires and seeking nothing for himself—
how could he engage in dispute with people?”
“Householder, this is how the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One should be understood in detail.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“Having abandoned the home, wandering without a fixed abode,”
The sage who forms no intimacies in the village,
free from sensual desires and seeking nothing for himself—
how could he engage in dispute with people?
One who wanders alone and secluded in the world should not speak while grasping at those things,
just as a noble elephant [does not grasp] the lotus growing in the mud or the one born in the water.
Unstained by water or mud,
even so the sage who speaks of peace, being free from greed,
is unstained by sensual pleasures and the world.
"One should wander secluded from those things in this world":
"from those" means from those views.
"Secluded" means empty of, secluded from, and withdrawn from bodily misconduct; [secluded] from verbal misconduct...
He is empty of, secluded from, and withdrawn from mental misconduct … from lust … [and so on] … from all unwholesome volitional formations.
"Should wander about" means: he should wander, dwell, conduct himself, behave, protect, support, and maintain himself.
"In the world" means: in the human world—that world from which he should wander, being secluded.
One should not speak of them as having grasped [the fetters], saying "he is no nāga.
He is called a *nāga* because he does not commit transgressions (*āguṃ na karoti*),
and he is called a *nāga* because he does not go [to states of woe].
A nāga is so called because he does not come (na āgacchati).
How does he not come? He does not come [to rebirth] by way of evil deeds. Thus he is a nāga.
What is a *nāga*?
Evil, unwholesome states are called *āgu*: they are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death.
He does nothing in the world that is an *āgu*.
(To Sabhiya, the Blessed One said:
Having cast off all fetters and bonds,
he is liberated and does not cling anywhere.
A "nāga" is so called because of being such;
thus, because he does not commit an offense (āgu),
he is a nāga.
How does he not go astray—
being a nāga?
He does not go astray through desire, he does not go astray through hatred, he does not go astray through delusion, and he does not go astray through fear.
He goes; he does not go under the influence of lust, he does not go under the influence of hatred, he does not go under the influence of delusion,
he does not go under the influence of conceit, he does not go under the influence of views,

he does not go under the influence of restlessness, he does not go under the influence of doubt, he does not go under the influence of underlying tendencies, and he is not carried away or led astray by factional doctrines.
It is carried away and swept along.
Thus, "he does not go"— therefore he is called a *nāga*.
How is it that he does not come back, thus he is a *nāga*?
By means of the stream-entry path, those defilements which have been abandoned— he does not bring them back, does not return to them, does not go back to them.
By means of the path of once-returning...
by means of the path of non-returning...
by means of the path of arahantship, those defilements that have been abandoned are not repeated, do not recur, and do not return.
Thus he does not come [to rebirth],
hence he is a "nāga. One should not say, "He is a nāga," by merely seizing upon those [characteristics].
Nāga would not, having grasped, mastered, taken up, clung to, and adhered to those speculative views, say, speak, declare, explain, or express:
"The world is eternal...
[and so on] ...the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—thus he would not say, speak, declare, explain, or express it.
A noble one (nāga) would not speak by grasping at those things, just as a lotus (*elambuja*) born in the mud of a pond is unsullied by water or mud.

"Water" (*ela*) is said to mean water; "lotus" (*ambuja*) is said to mean a *paduma*; "thorny stalk" (*kaṇḍaka*) is said to mean a rough stem; "water" (*vāri*) is said to mean water; "born in water" (*vārija*) is said to mean a *paduma* produced from water; "liquid" (*jala*) is said to mean water; and "mud" (*paṅka*) is said to mean mire.
Just as a lotus born in water, arisen from water, is not smeared, nor defiled, nor stained by water or mud— being unsmeared, undefiled, and unstained—
just as this water-born *elambuja* and *kaṇḍaka* lotus is unstained by water and mud;
even so the sage, a speaker of peace, being free from greed, is unstained by sensual pleasures and the world.
Thus is the application of the simile.
“The Sage” (muni): “Mona” is said to be knowledge … [as above] … having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.

“Peaceful in speech”: the sage speaks of peace, speaks of refuge, speaks of shelter, speaks of sanctuary, speaks of fearlessness, speaks of the deathless, speaks of the immortal, speaks of Nibbāna—in this way the sage is peaceful in speech.
He is free from greed.
"Greed" is said to be craving.
It is that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
One for whom this greed has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one free from greed."
Thus, he is not greedy for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clans,
assemblies, dwellings, gains, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, the realm of sensual desire,
the realm of form, the realm of the formless, the existence of sensual desire, the existence of form, or the existence of the formless.

In the realm of perception … in the realm of non-perception … in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception … in the realm of one constituent … in the realm of four constituents … in the realm of five constituents … in the past … in the future … in the present … regarding phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and cognized— he is not greedy,
not infatuated, not deluded, and not obsessed; he is free from greed, devoid of greed, having abandoned greed, and having overcome greed.
With craving for existence abandoned, with craving relinquished, he is free from passion, devoid of passion, with passion cast out, passion vomited up, passion released, passion abandoned,
and craving relinquished; hungerless, extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss,
he dwells having become, by himself, one who has become sublime.
Thus the sage, a speaker of peace, free from greed,
is unsullied by sensual pleasures and by the world.
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā), in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures:
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
"World" means the world of the states of misery, the world of humans, the world of gods, the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, and the world of the sense bases.
"Smearing" refers to two kinds of smearing:
the smearing of craving and the smearing of views... [etc.]
This is the smear of craving... [and so on] ...this is the smear of views.
Having abandoned the smear of craving and relinquished the smear of views, the sage does not smear himself with sense pleasures or the world.
He does not smear himself, nor does he defile himself; unsmeared, undefiled, and untainted, he dwells with a mind that has gone forth, escaped, is liberated, detached, and free from boundaries—
a sage who speaks of peace, free from greed, and unsmeared by both sensual pleasures and the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those things by which one might wander detached in the world—
the Naga would not speak of them, having grasped at them.”
Just as a lotus born in a muddy pond is unsullied by water or mud, so the sage,
who speaks of peace and is free from greed, remains unstained.
“Unstained by sensual pleasures and by the world.
The possessor of knowledge does not rely on view nor on wisdom;
he does not esteem himself, for he is not made of that.
He cannot be led by action nor by learning;
he is not drawn into worldly abodes.
He is neither a master of Vedic knowledge nor one who clings to views, nor does he rely on mere logic; such a one does not harbor pride.
This is not a negation.
"Vedagu" means this:
"Veda" refers to the knowledge in the four paths; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment, inquiry, insight, and right view.
By those knowledges, he has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; he has attained the end, reached the limit, attained the limit,
reached the boundary, attained the boundary, reached the finality, attained the finality, reached security, attained security,
reached shelter, attained shelter, reached refuge, attained refuge, reached fearlessness, attained fearlessness, and reached the deathless, attained the deathless.
One who has attained the deathless; one who has reached Nibbāna, one who has attained Nibbāna; or, because he has gone to the end of the Vedas, he is a "Vedagū";
or, because he has gone to the end by means of the Vedas, he is a "Vedagū"; or, because of his having known seven things, he is a "Vedagū":
namely, personality-belief is known, doubt is known, adherence to rites and rituals is known, lust is known, and hatred... [is known].
Delusion is known, pride is known, and those evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence,
accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death, are known by him.
Having discriminated all the Vedas, [he knows them to be empty].
(To Sabhiya, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever [qualities] belong to recluses and brahmins,
[I am] free from passion toward all feelings."
"Having transcended all knowledge, he is a master of knowledge.
Regarding "not by views": his sixty-two types of speculative views have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
He is not led away, carried off, swept away, or dragged along by view; nor does he regard that speculative view as essential, nor does he return to it.

"Not by learning, not by views, not by wisdom"—meaning he does not lead pride forward, does not approach it, does not go toward it, does not grasp it, does not misapprehend it, and does not adhere to it, whether by way of wisdom, or by another's voice, or by the conventional consensus of the multitude. Thus:
"Not by learning, not by views, not by wisdom does he lead pride. He does not lead pride by means of wisdom.
For he is not "made of that" (tammaya) by way of craving or by way of views; he does not have that as his supreme goal, nor that as his resort.

Since craving, views, and conceit have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future—to this extent he is not made of that, does not have that as his supreme goal, and does not have that as his resort.
Thus, "he does not conceive conceit," for he is not made of that.
"Neither by action nor by learning is one led. "Not by action" means:
one does not go, is not led, is not carried away, and is not swept along by either the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, or the formation of the imperturbable;
thus, "not by action."

"Nor is he led by what is heard": by means of the purity of what is heard, or by the voice of another, or by the consensus of the multitude, he is not led, not carried away, not swept along, and not drawn hither and thither;
thus, "nor is he led by what is heard. "He is not led into abodes": he is not led into states of existence.
There are two kinds of clinging:
clinging to craving and clinging to views... [as before] ...this is clinging to craving... [as before] ...
This is the resort of views.
For him, the resort of craving has been abandoned and the resort of views has been relinquished.
Because the resort of craving has been abandoned and the resort of views has been relinquished, he is not led into and is unsullied by worldly attachments.

"Not having approached, not being attached, not being intent upon, having gone out from, having escaped, being liberated, and being dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries"—
thus he is "not led into" dwellings.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The one who has realized the truth is not led by views nor by wisdom;
he does not esteem himself, for he is not made of that.
He cannot be led by action, nor even by learning.”
"He has not been led into household dwellings.
For one who is dispassionate toward perceptions, there are no fetters;
for one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions.
Those who have grasped at perception and views wander about in the world, clashing with others;
for one who is dispassionate toward perception, there are no fetters.
For one who develops the noble path preceded by serenity, from the very beginning the fetters are suppressed; and when arahantship is attained,
for the arahant the fetters, delusions, hindrances, the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, the perception of cruelty,
and the perception of views are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and rendered incapable of future arising.
"Subject to non-arising in the future"—
for one who is dispassionate toward perception, there are no fetters;
for one liberated by wisdom, there is no delusion.
For one who develops the Noble Path preceded by insight, from the very beginning their delusion is suppressed;
and upon reaching Arahantship, for the Arahant, delusion, the fetters, the hindrances, the perception of sensual desire,
the perception of ill will, the perception of cruelty, and the perception of views are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and rendered incapable of future arising.
"Those things that are subject to non-arising in the future—
for one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions.
Those who have grasped at perception and views wander about, clashing with one another in the world."
Those who grasp at perceptions—perceptions of sensual desire, perceptions of ill will, and perceptions of cruelty—clash and collide because of those perceptions.
Kings dispute with kings, kshatriyas dispute with kshatriyas, brahmins dispute with brahmins, householders dispute with householders;
even a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother.
They quarrel: the father quarrels with the son, the son quarrels with the father;
the brother quarrels with the brother, the sister quarrels with the sister, the brother quarrels with the sister, the sister quarrels with the brother;
even a companion quarrels with a companion.
Having fallen there into quarrels, disputes, and contention, they attack one another with their hands, they attack with clods of earth, they attack with sticks, and they attack with weapons.
There they undergo even death or suffering amounting to death.
Those who take up the view that "the world is eternal," or [as it continues]...
Or, by way of the view that "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death," they clash and collide;
they clash teacher with teacher, teaching with teaching, group with group, view with view, practice with practice, and path with path.
Or else they dispute, quarrel, bicker, contend, argue, and create strife, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya...
[and so on] ...either explain it yourself, if you are able."
Their volitional formations are not abandoned;
because volitional formations are not abandoned, they are impelled toward a destination:

they are impelled toward hell, they are impelled toward the animal realm, they are impelled toward the sphere of hungry ghosts, they are impelled toward the world of humans, they are impelled toward the world of devas, [and] toward a destination.

They strike against one another, collide, speak, move about, dwell, conduct themselves, turn, protect, maintain, sustain, and endure from destiny to destiny, from rebirth to rebirth, from rebirth-linking to rebirth-linking, from existence to existence, from saṃsāra to saṃsāra, and from the round of existence to the round of existence.
"In the world"— that is, in the world of the lower realms …pe… in the world of the sense bases—
those who have grasped at perception and view wander about in the world, clashing with one another.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one detached from perception, there are no fetters;
for one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions.
But those who have grasped at perception and views—”
“They wander about in the world, clashing with one another.
Thus ends the ninth exposition, the *Māgaṇḍiya-sutta-niddesa*.
